document.note: English translation of Gen. Lyakhovsky's authoritative section on Soviet decisions on Afghanistan in December 1979, based on near-complete access to Defense Ministry and Central Committee records. It covers Ustinov's agreement with Andropov and the 75,000-troop plan, and cites threats such as U.S. missiles, CIA activity and possible Pakistani annexation.

events.description: Narrow Politburo meeting in Brezhnev's office on Afghanistan; two options drafted: remove Amin via KGB and install Karmal, or send troops.
Ustinov instructs Ogarkov to prepare 75-80 thousand troops; Ogarkov objects; small Politburo session tentatively orders preparation; Defense Ministry Collegium informed.
Politburo unanimously decides to introduce Soviet troops into Afghanistan, termed 'the measures'; protocol handwritten by Chernenko.
Narrow Politburo meeting in Brezhnev's office discusses introducing Soviet troops; two options developed (remove Amin via KGB, or send troops).
Ustinov summons Ogarkov, orders preparation of 75-80 thousand troops; Ogarkov objects.
Ogarkov summoned to 'small Politburo' in Brezhnev's office; preparations ordered but no final decision.
Ustinov gathers Defense Ministry Collegium; Directive #312/12/00133 sent to troops; formation of new Army in Turkestan Military District begins.
Ustinov summons Gen. Zaplatin to Moscow to report on the Afghan army.
Politburo unanimously decides to introduce Soviet troops into Afghanistan, codenamed 'the measures'; Kosygin absent; protocol handwritten by Chernenko.

sources_cited: Alexander Lyakhovsky, The Tragedy and Valor of Afghan (GPI Iskon, Moscow, 1995)
Protocol of 12 December 1979 Politburo session (handwritten by Chernenko)
key_claims: The Politburo's inner circle (Andropov, Ustinov, Gromyko) initiated and made the final decision on 12 December 1979 to send troops into Afghanistan.
Ogarkov, the Chief of General Staff, opposed the intervention as 'reckless' but was overruled.
Soviet justifications included alleged CIA plans, possible US Pershing missiles in Afghanistan, Afghan uranium, and Pakistani annexation of the north.
A KGB report from Kabul by B. Ivanov was decisive and overrode Zaplatin's dissent about dramatized assessments.
Kosygin opposed the decision and did not attend; orders were given orally with no Supreme Soviet decree, partly to confuse Amin.
